desc:
You may append any number of lowercase letters to the end of the string s. Return the smallest number of letters you must append so that t becomes a subsequence of the resulting string.

A subsequence is obtained by deleting zero or more characters without changing the order of the rest.

For example, with s = "abracadabra" and t = "arcade" the letters a r c a d can already be found in order inside s, only the final e is missing, so the answer is 1. With s = "xyz" and t = "abc" nothing matches, so the answer is 3.
constraints: Both strings consist of lowercase English letters
hints: If you append a copy of the unmatched tail of t, that tail is certainly a subsequence of the new string. The only question is how long the tail has to be.
A longer matched prefix of t inside s means a shorter tail. Which prefix of t is the longest one that is a subsequence of s?
Scan s once with a pointer j into t; whenever s[i] == t[j], advance j. The answer is len(t) - j.
editorial: Let j be the length of the longest prefix of t that is a subsequence of s. The remaining len(t) - j letters of t must come after everything in s that was used for the prefix; appending exactly those letters is always enough, so the answer is at most len(t) - j.

It cannot be smaller: if fewer letters were appended, the matched part of t inside s would have to be longer than j, contradicting that j is the longest matchable prefix. The greedy scan (match the earliest possible position for every letter of t) finds that longest prefix. It runs in O(|s|) time and O(1) space.
